title: Leaving Canada? What happens to your taxes
seo_title: Leaving Canada: Tax Guide for Emigrants and Departure Tax
description: Becoming a non-resident, your final return, departure tax, T1161 and T1244, withholding on Canadian income, and your RRSP, TFSA and FHSA.
lead: Moving abroad changes how Canada taxes you, and the year you leave has its own rules and forms. Here's what to sort out before and after you go.
key_points: You usually become a non-resident on the latest of the day you leave, the day your family leaves, or the day you become a resident of your new country.
Your final return reports world income up to your departure date and only certain Canadian income after it.
Most property is treated as sold at market value when you leave, but Canadian real estate and registered plans like RRSPs and TFSAs are not.
File Form T1161 if everything you own is worth more than $25,000; you can put off paying departure tax with Form T1244.
After you leave, Canadian payers usually hold back 25% of income like rent, pensions and RRSP withdrawals, unless a tax treaty lowers it.
Don't contribute to your TFSA once you are a non-resident, and deal with any HBP or LLP balance within 60 days of leaving.

sections.heading: When you stop being a Canadian resident
sections.html:
Canada taxes people based on residency, not citizenship. You become an emigrant for tax when you leave Canada to live in another country and cut your residential ties, which are the links between your life and Canada.

  • Significant ties: a home in Canada, a spouse or common-law partner in Canada, and dependants (such as children) in Canada.
  • Secondary ties: personal property such as a car or furniture, social ties such as club or religious memberships, economic ties such as Canadian bank accounts and credit cards, a Canadian driver's licence, a Canadian passport, and provincial health insurance.

Cutting ties usually means giving up your Canadian home, setting up a permanent home abroad, and having your spouse and children move too.

How the CRA may see you

StatusWhat it means
Factual residentYou live abroad for a while but keep residential ties here. You are still taxed as a resident.
Deemed non-residentYou still have ties to Canada, but under a tax treaty (an agreement between two countries) you count as a resident of the other country. The same rules as for emigrants apply.
Non-resident (emigrant)You have no significant ties left. Canada taxes only certain Canadian income.
Deemed residentYou have no significant ties, but you stay in Canada for 183 days or more in the year. You are taxed as a resident.

If your situation is unclear, you can ask the CRA for its opinion with Form NR73, Determination of Residency Status (leaving Canada). This form is optional.

sections.heading: Your departure date
sections.html:
Your departure date is the day you become a non-resident. It is usually the latest of these dates:

  • the day you leave Canada;
  • the day your spouse or common-law partner and dependants leave Canada;
  • the day you become a resident of the country where you settle.

Example (for illustration only): you fly to your new country on June 1, but your spouse and children stay to finish the school year and join you on July 15. Your departure date is usually July 15.

Exception: if you lived in another country before and are going back there, you usually become a non-resident on the day you leave, even if your spouse stays behind for a while to sell your home.

Even if you don't need to file a return for the year you leave, tell the CRA your departure date as soon as you can.

sections.heading: Your final (departure-year) tax return
sections.html:
In the year you leave, you file a return that covers two periods. Enter your departure date on page 1, and use the BC forms if you lived in BC on that date.

  • Before you left: report your world income (Canadian and foreign income) in Canadian dollars.
  • After you left: some Canadian income still goes on the return, such as pay for work done in Canada, business income in Canada and gains on certain Canadian property. Other Canadian income, like dividends, rent and pensions, is usually handled by tax held back by the payer (see below).

Credits and deductions

  • Non-refundable credits (credits that lower your tax but can't create a refund on their own, such as the basic personal amount) are worked out for the time you were a resident and the time you weren't, so you may get less than a full-year resident. Some BC credits are limited in the same way.
  • Most deductions still apply, but moving expenses for a move abroad generally don't, except for some full-time students with a taxable Canadian scholarship or grant.
  • Provincial refundable credits (ones that can be paid to you) are generally not available unless you were a Canadian resident on December 31.

Due dates

The return is due April 30 of the year after you leave, or June 15 if you or your spouse or common-law partner carried on a business in Canada. Any balance owing is due by April 30 either way. For example, if you leave in 2026, the usual deadline is April 30, 2027.

sections.heading: Departure tax: the deemed sale of your property
sections.html:
When you leave, the CRA treats you as if you sold most of your property on your departure date at its fair market value (FMV), the price it would fetch on the open market, and bought it straight back. This deemed disposition is often called "departure tax": you may owe tax on a capital gain (the increase in value) even though you sold nothing.

Example (round numbers for illustration): you bought shares in a regular, non-registered account for $20,000, and they are worth $50,000 when you leave. You report a $30,000 capital gain on your final return.

Property that is not deemed sold

  • Canadian real estate, such as your house, condo or rental property, plus Canadian resource and timber property. It stays taxable in Canada when you actually sell it later.
  • Canadian business property, if you carry on the business through a permanent establishment (a fixed place of business) in Canada.
  • Registered plans and pensions: pension plans and annuities, RRSPs, RRIFs, PRPPs, RESPs, RDSPs, TFSAs, employee stock options that are subject to Canadian tax, and life insurance policies in Canada (other than segregated fund policies).
  • Short-term residents: if you lived in Canada for 60 months or less in the 10 years before you leave, property you owned when you last arrived (or inherited after arriving) is not deemed sold.

The forms

  • Form T1243, Deemed Disposition of Property by an Emigrant of Canada, works out the gains and losses. You then carry them to Schedule 3 of your return.
  • Form T1161, List of Properties by an Emigrant of Canada, is required if the total FMV of everything you owned when you left is more than $25,000. Leave out cash and bank deposits, registered plans, and personal-use items (such as household goods, clothing and cars) worth less than $10,000 each. It is due by your filing due date, even if you don't otherwise need to file a return. Filing it late costs $25 a day, with a minimum of $100 and a maximum of $2,500.

Putting off the tax: Form T1244

You can choose to defer (put off) paying departure tax until you actually sell the property, with no interest, by filing Form T1244 by April 30 of the year after you leave. If the federal tax you are deferring is more than $16,500, you must give the CRA adequate security (something that guarantees payment), and you may need security for provincial tax too. Contact the CRA early to arrange it.

Get values on your departure date. Save statements showing what each investment was worth the day you left. If you later move back and still own the property, you may be able to elect to undo the deemed sale, and you will need these numbers.

sections.heading: Canadian income after you leave
sections.html:
Non-resident tax (Part XIII)

Once you are a non-resident, Canadian payers must hold back non-resident tax (called Part XIII tax) on income such as dividends, rent, pensions, Old Age Security (OAS), Canada Pension Plan (CPP) benefits, RRSP and RRIF payments, and annuities. The usual rate is 25%, unless a tax treaty between Canada and your new country lowers it. Interest paid by an arm's-length payer, such as an ordinary bank, is generally exempt. You get an NR4 slip showing what was paid and held back. This is usually your final Canadian tax on that income, so you generally don't file a return for it.

The section 217 election

If you receive pension-type income from Canada, such as OAS, CPP, most workplace pensions, most RRSP and RRIF income, or Employment Insurance (EI) benefits, you can choose to file a Canadian return under section 217. That income is then taxed at the same rates as for residents, and you may get back some or all of the 25% held back. The CRA applies the election only if it helps you. The return must be filed by June 30 of the next year, or the CRA can't accept the election; any balance owing is still due April 30. If you receive OAS while living abroad, you may also need to file Form T1136 each year. See our retirement income guide.

Keeping a Canadian rental property

  • Your tenant or agent (such as a property manager) must hold back 25% of the gross rent and send it to the CRA by the 15th of the next month.
  • If you and your agent file Form NR6 and the CRA approves it, the 25% is held back from the net rent (rent minus expenses) instead. File it on or before January 1 each year, or before the first rent payment is due.
  • Under section 216 you can file a separate rental income return, paying tax on the net profit and getting back extra tax held back. If you used an NR6, this return is due June 30 of the next year. Without an NR6, you have two years from the end of the year the rent was paid to file it.

Selling Canadian property later

When a non-resident sells taxable Canadian property, such as Canadian real estate, you must tell the CRA before the sale or within 10 days after it, usually with Form T2062. You pay 25% of the gain, or give security, and the CRA then issues a certificate of compliance. Without one, the buyer can be on the hook for 25% of the price (50% for some kinds of property) and may hold that back. Late notice costs $25 a day, at least $100 and up to $2,500. In most cases you also file a return for the year of sale by April 30 of the next year. Our capital gains guide explains the gain.

sections.heading: Your RRSP, TFSA, FHSA, HBP and LLP
sections.html:
AccountWhat happens when you leave
RRSP / RRIFNot deemed sold, so you can keep it. Payments after you leave have 25% non-resident tax held back (less if a treaty applies). A section 217 election may lower the tax.
TFSAYou can keep it, and its income and withdrawals aren't taxed in Canada. You get no new room for any full year you are a non-resident. Withdrawals made while you are away are added back to your room only if you become a resident again.
FHSAYou can keep it, but you can't make a tax-free withdrawal to buy a home while you are a non-resident. Taxable withdrawals have 25% held back, unless a treaty lowers it.
Home Buyers' Plan (HBP)If you already bought the home, repay the balance by the earlier of when you file your return for the year you leave, or 60 days after you become a non-resident. Otherwise, the balance is added to that year's income.
Lifelong Learning Plan (LLP)Same deadline: repay the balance, or it is added to your income for the year you leave.
Don't contribute to your TFSA after you leave. A contribution made while you are a non-resident is taxed at 1% for each month it stays in the account, until you withdraw it or move back. Your new country may also tax TFSA income and withdrawals, so check its rules.

sections.heading: Benefits, banks and other loose ends
sections.html:
• Benefits stop. As a non-resident you are generally not eligible for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit or the Canada child benefit, including related provincial payments. Tell the CRA your departure date. If payments keep arriving after you leave, contact the CRA right away.
  • Tell your banks and payers. Let every Canadian bank, brokerage, pension plan and other payer know you are no longer a resident, so they hold back the right tax and send you NR4 slips.
  • Keep records of your departure date, property values and returns, and keep your address up to date with the CRA.

sections.heading: Checklist before and after you leave
sections.html:
1. Work out your departure date and keep proof (tickets, lease or sale papers, residence papers from your new country).
  2. Check whether you are really cutting your ties; use NR73 if you want the CRA's view.
  3. Get the fair market value of your investments and other property on your departure date.
  4. Complete T1243 and, if everything you own is worth more than $25,000, T1161.
  5. Decide whether to defer departure tax with T1244 (by April 30 of the next year), and arrange security if the federal tax is over $16,500.
  6. Repay any HBP or LLP balance within 60 days of leaving (or before you file, if sooner), or plan for the tax.
  7. Stop TFSA contributions from your departure date.
  8. If you keep a rental, choose an agent and file NR6 before rent starts.
  9. Tell the CRA, your banks and other payers that you are a non-resident.
  10. File your final return by April 30 of the year after you leave (June 15 if you ran a business in Canada).

Leaving with investments, a home or registered plans means several one-time decisions, so plan them before you go. If you later return, see our newcomers guide.
